Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: Known hyperthyroidism; long-standing high-stress professional role; recent job change
- Precipitating factors: Acute work-related stress and increased cognitive/visual load (reading/meetings/computer work)
- Perpetuating factors: Ongoing work demands, potential thyroid status instability if thyroxine dosing is inappropriate, appetite/weight changes
- Protective factors: Engagement with primary care; willingness to pursue in-person evaluation
- Overall: Symptom cluster (headache with nausea; tachycardia; heat sensation; dyspnea; weight loss; reduced appetite; decreased libido; arm tingling) in context of known hyperthyroidism and substantial work stress—brought to clinical attention for medical evaluation and targeted testing; differential includes thyrotoxicosis, anxiety/panic-related autonomic arousal, and headache disorders

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem:
- Patient Goal(s): Obtain comprehensive medical evaluation and diagnostic testing; address symptoms that affect work performance; understand thyroid status; discuss potential anxiety components; proceed with in-person clinic assessment
- Clinical Goal(s): Rule in/out hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis with thyroid function testing; evaluate autonomic symptoms and headaches; assess for anxiety-related contributions; plan appropriate medical and possible psychological interventions
- Actions (Patient): Attend in-person clinic appointment; complete ordered blood tests (TSH, Free T4, thyroid antibodies as indicated); monitor symptoms; report new or worsening symptoms; maintain current thyroid medication unless advised otherwise
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Conduct physical examination focusing on cardiovascular and thyroid systems; order labs (including TSH, Free T4, T3 if needed, CBC, metabolic panel); consider baseline ECG if tachycardia/dyspnea persist; review and adjust thyroxine therapy as indicated; provide medical management and referrals as indicated (Endocrinology if persistent thyrotoxicosis; possible neurology or headache specialist; consider brief mental health evaluation if anxiety symptoms persist); arrange follow-up

Secondary Problem (if applicable):
- Patient Goal(s): Understand and manage anxiety/autonomic symptoms in relation to work stress
- Clinical Goal(s): Identify contributing psychosocial factors; provide coping strategies and consider referral if indicated
- Actions (Patient): Engage in recommended coping strategies; participate in follow-up planning
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Offer brief psychoeducation on stress management; assess need for behavioral health referral; monitor symptom trajectory

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Thyrotoxicosis / Hyperthyroidism (likely due to levothyroxine therapy; Glad to rule in/out with testing)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Known hyperthyroidism; tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, reduced appetite, libido decrease align with thyrotoxicosis; symptom onset after job change supports a stress context but thyroid status remains a coherent explanation
- Anxiety/panic disorder with autonomic symptoms related to work stress
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: High work-related stress (7–8/10), episodic tachycardia, brief dyspnea, arm tingling, and symptom fluctuation fit autonomic arousal
- Migraine-type or tension-type headache with autonomic features
  - Likelihood: Medium-High
  - Justification: Frontal headaches with nausea occurring during work; correlation with prolonged computer/reading tasks; autonomic symptoms and episodic nature support a headache disorder
- (Low likelihood) Pheochromocytoma
  - Likelihood: Low
  - Justification: Paroxysmal headaches with tachycardia and weight loss could occur with pheochromocytoma, but absence of hypertension, diaphoresis, or classic triad lowers probability
